doc.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven records
summary: Gordon calls the Hot Five and Hot Seven records milestones, and recalls Gennett recording stopping when trains passed.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Great. You’ve mentioned the “Hot Five” and “Hot Seven” a couple of times. What was it about those particular recordings that really were such milestones, in your eyes?

In the first place they were called “race records” I guess they were called. They all sold a million records. Each copy that came out on 78s. And Louis Armstrong was just a genius of a cornet player on those records. That was just a recording band. They never played out in a club or anything like that. All they did was get together to record. And I think Louis Armstrong really showed the whole world, including today, everybody that’s playing trumpet, Louis Armstrong had an influence on everybody, and especially at that time when he was 25 or 26 or 27 years old. He was just playing some marvelous stuff on there, I thought, along with his contemporaries, Johnny Dodds and Kid Ory and the other ones that were on the records with him.
The sound of the instruments that come off those old 78s is interesting. The technology of the time kind of flavored what everything sounded like.

Well they used to record in Hammond, Indiana I think and they had — for Gennett Records — back in the 20s. And there was a train that would go by every day, two or three times a day, so they had to stop recording when the train went by. They were in a little barn and everything shut down when the train went by and then they’d get back and start recording again.
